entries.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A nine-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's covering assertion' (credited to OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims that X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴, |u| = 1}, the set of rank-one orthogonal projectors on ℝ⁴ inside the nine-dimensional trace-one affine space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices with the Frobenius metric, has diameter √2 and cannot be covered by ten subsets of diameter strictly less than √2. Its main theorem states this and writes it as b(X) > 10, where b(Y) is the least number of pieces of strictly smaller diameter needed to cover Y. The same manuscript's corollary extends this to every dimension d ≥ 9: for each such d there is a compact subset of ℝᵈ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by d+1 subsets of strictly smaller diameter. It is built from a translate of X in ℝ⁹ together with s = d−9 further points, which lie at mutual distance √2 from each other and from every point of the translate (vectors with Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ). The proof of the main theorem is topological and combinatorial. A cover by pieces of diameter below √2 yields a smooth partition of unity on ℝP³ whose positive supports are disjoint for orthogonal lines. Extending the resulting map to symmetric matrices gives an odd map from the 9-sphere to the 9-sphere. Its mod-two degree forces every maximal support to have four labels, with their sum a simplicial cycle. Degree and double-cover counts then force a six-label triangle system on the complement of each tetrahedral support, and a combinatorial analysis of these systems across adjacent tetrahedra gives a contradiction, so no admissible map ℝP³ → Δ⁹ exists.
entries.delivers: For the bullet's lower-bound part: the manuscript exhibits a compact set in ℝ⁹ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by ten pieces of strictly smaller diameter, so the minimum number of pieces for that set is at least 11, i.e. f(9) ≥ 11. By the corollary, for every d ≥ 9 some compact set in ℝᵈ needs at least d+2 pieces, giving f(d) ≥ d+2 for all d ≥ 9. This disproves the conjecture that d+1 pieces always suffice in each of those dimensions. Restrictions: the bounds are lower bounds only, and they apply to d ≥ 9. The manuscript says nothing about dimensions 8 and below and does not claim the conjecture fails there. The examples have diameter √2 rather than 1; the piece count is unchanged by scaling. The manuscript states the covering form, which matches the list's wording. It also remarks that covers and partitions give the same count, because overlaps can be removed without increasing diameters. That remark bears on the cover-versus-partition question the frozen statement leaves open. The manuscript does not claim to settle the problem. It says the theorem 'does not determine the smallest dimension in which it fails or the exact value of b(X)'.
entries.remains: If the claim is correct, still open: the exact value of f(n) in every dimension, and the exact value of b(X) (only b(X) > 10 is proved). Also open: the smallest dimension in which the covering assertion fails, including whether it fails in any dimension from 2 to 8, which the manuscript does not address. Every upper bound on f(n) is open; the manuscript gives none. The growth of f(n) as n increases is open too: the manuscript's only new bound is the linear lower bound n+2.
entries.direction: disproves the conjecture f(n) = n+1 for every n ≥ 9 (lower bound f(n) ≥ n+2)
entries.object: The set X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴ unit}, the image of ℝP³ under u ↦ uuᵀ, is explicit. The manuscript gives an explicit isometry from its trace-one matrix space to ℝ⁹ in a remark on Euclidean coordinates. Its non-coverability is proved by a contradiction argument, not by an explicit certificate. For d ≥ 10 the added points are given by the explicit Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ, which determines them up to an orthogonal change of basis.
entries.doubts: (1) The non-coverability proof is a long hand argument spanning the geometry, topology, six-label and ten-label sections. The text reports no computer check. (2) Several combinatorial steps are compressed into a sentence and are not flagged as sketched: the 'realizes every possible choice of omissions' step in the partner-block lemma; the claim in the two-tetrahedra lemma that the transported systems 'agree everywhere' from agreement on five labels; and, in the six-label lemma, the statement that a perpendicular line 'could use none of the six labels', where the contradiction also uses that a line's coordinates sum to one, which the text leaves implicit. (3) The claim that the result improves the dimension bound from 63 rests on a cited public note (Grinsztajn 2026), which the manuscript neither proves nor uses in its argument.
